title: Crisis response is being reframed as development from day one, linking services, livelihoods, institutions, peacebuilding, and climate resilience
source_unit: UNDP, Moving Beyond Crisis: Action Agenda
geography: Global crisis-affected, fragile, conflict-affected, and disaster-exposed settings, with national and local systems as the intended delivery base

acute_poverty_in_crisis.unit: people in acute poverty living in countries affected by war, fragility, or low peacefulness

crisis_armed_groups.unit: non-state armed groups controlling territory worldwide, approximately

observations.method: UNDP compiles global conflict, poverty, displacement, climate, disaster, health, and governance indicators to frame the convergence of crisis pressures and development reversals.
observations.uncertainty: The figures use different years, definitions, and source systems; they describe overlapping global conditions and should not be summed or treated as one joint population count.
observations.subgroup: People in conflict and fragile settings, displaced populations, low-income households, host communities, public institutions, local authorities, and humanitarian and development actors.
observations.counterinterpretation: Global crisis indicators can obscure local resilience, uneven exposure, and differences between acute emergency need, chronic fragility, and recoverable shock.

action_fronts.value: prepare and prevent; respond and recover; transition and transform

development_shift.value: restore essential services, livelihoods, infrastructure, governance, rule of law, and social cohesion from the outset of crisis

transition_logic.value: shift leadership, responsibility, and resources progressively to affected communities and national and local institutions

observations.method: The Action Agenda organizes UNDP's contribution across prevention, response, recovery, transition, and transformation rather than assuming a single linear crisis sequence.
observations.uncertainty: The model is a programmatic framework, not evidence that day-one development action produces faster recovery or prevents relapse in every setting.
observations.subgroup: Crisis-affected communities, national and local institutions, humanitarian agencies, peacebuilding actors, development partners, and groups facing exclusion from recovery decisions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Early development programming can protect systems and agency, but it can also divert resources from immediate life-saving needs or impose external institutional models if locally led transition is weak.

building_blocks.value: analytics; services, infrastructure and institutions; livelihoods, jobs and economies; peacebuilding and social cohesion; climate and nature

reinforcement_path.value: restored services support livelihoods, livelihoods support social cohesion, and stronger institutions rebuild confidence in the social contract

finance.value: crisis-ready finance and earlier risk-informed investment are treated as cross-cutting requirements

observations.method: UNDP presents the five building blocks as mutually reinforcing components that should be adapted to context across the three action fronts.
observations.uncertainty: The proposed reinforcement pathway is a theory of action, not a quantified causal model or implementation assessment across countries.
observations.subgroup: Public service users, workers, firms, local economies, social-cohesion actors, climate-vulnerable communities, and institutions managing recovery finance.
observations.counterinterpretation: Integrated programming can improve coherence while creating coordination burdens, blurred accountability, and competition among sectoral priorities.

observations.period: 2025-2026; financing and system-capacity constraints on crisis recovery

oda_change.unit: percent change in official development assistance in 2025, as reported

debt_interest_constraint.unit: people living in countries spending more on debt interest than on health or education

natural_catastrophe_losses.unit: US dollars in economic losses from natural catastrophes in 2024, with 63 percent uninsured

resource_problem.value: response resources are contracting while crisis needs rise

observations.method: The Action Agenda combines macro-finance, disaster-loss, aid-flow, debt, and crisis-need indicators to argue for earlier, more resilient, and differently financed development action.
observations.uncertainty: The indicators come from different sources and do not estimate the counterfactual effect of financing changes or identify which actors can close each gap.
observations.subgroup: Low-income and crisis-affected countries, debt-constrained public systems, uninsured households and firms, displaced people, donors, development financiers, and local recovery institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Reduced aid can encourage domestic ownership or new financing arrangements, while early investment can fail if governance, conflict, or fiduciary conditions remain unresolved.

related_sources.claim: UNDP trends update context on development risks and structural transitions.
Related UNDP-UNU framework on service delivery and non-state actors in complex settings.

boundary: This record adds a crisis-development systems route linking conflict, displacement, climate shocks, debt and aid constraints, essential services, livelihoods, institutions, social cohesion, and locally led transition. It is a UNDP action framework with aggregate contextual indicators, not a complete crisis census, respondent-level recovery histories, causal evaluation, funding audit, or proof that development-from-day-one programming works uniformly across settings.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official 20-page UNDP Action Agenda and publication page were reviewed for crisis indicators, development-from-day-one framing, three action fronts, five building blocks, financing constraints, and the non-linear transition model.
